nameStory: The name 'peafowl' comes from the Latin 'pavo' meaning peacock, combined with 'fowl' for bird. 'Indian' refers to their native homeland in the Indian subcontinent, though they've been introduced worldwide as ornamental birds. The males are called peacocks, females are peahens, but most people just call them all peacocks!
description: Indian Peafowl are large, spectacular birds originally from India that have been introduced to many parts of the world, including some areas of New England. Males (peacocks) are famous for their brilliant blue and green plumage and enormous, fan-shaped tails covered in iridescent 'eye' spots. Females (peahens) are much more subdued, with brown feathers and smaller size. These ground-dwelling birds are about the size of a large turkey and are capable of flight despite their impressive plumage.

idTips.label: Male's spectacular tail display
idTips.description: The peacock's train of elongated feathers can spread into a massive fan covered with dozens of shimmering eye-spots that seem to watch you move - the feathers feel stiff and dry when touched, unlike soft body feathers

idTips.label: Bright blue head and neck
idTips.description: Males have an electric blue head and neck that looks almost metallic in sunlight, topped with a fan-shaped crest of delicate feathers that quiver when the bird moves

idTips.label: Loud, harsh calls
idTips.description: Their calls sound like a loud, piercing 'KEE-ow' or honking sound that can carry for miles - you'll often hear them long before you see them

idTips.label: Female's brown camouflage
idTips.description: Peahens are predominantly brown with intricate barring, a white face patch, and an iridescent green lower neck that catches the light when they turn their heads

idTips.label: Large ground-walking gait
idTips.description: They walk with a distinctive high-stepping, deliberate gait on strong legs, head bobbing forward and back like an oversized chicken

habitat: In New England, you'll find Indian Peafowl on private estates, farms, zoos, and occasionally as escaped birds in suburban areas with large yards. They prefer open areas near woodlands where they can forage on the ground but fly up into trees to roost at night. They need access to shelter and are often found near barns, sheds, or dense shrubs where they can escape predators.

seasonality.spring: Males are most spectacular in spring during breeding season, displaying their full tail fans and calling frequently to attract females.
seasonality.summer: Active foraging season when they're most visible on the ground, eating insects, small animals, and plant matter. Young birds may be seen following parents.
seasonality.fall: Males begin to molt their impressive tail feathers, making them less conspicuous. Birds gather in small groups and prepare for winter.
seasonality.winter: Tails are fully molted and males look much less impressive. They seek shelter near buildings and may be harder to spot as they conserve energy.

funFact: Despite having a tail that can be over 5 feet long and weighs several pounds, peacocks can still fly well enough to roost 40 feet high in trees - they're basically flying fashion statements with better aerial abilities than most people realize!
confusionNotes: The only real confusion might be with Wild Turkeys from a distance, but peacocks are much more colorful, have that distinctive crest, and make completely different sounds. Remember: if it's brown and big, it might be a turkey; if it's blue and fabulous, it's definitely a peacock!
contextualKnowledge: Many people don't realize that 'peacock' technically refers only to males - females are 'peahens' and the species collectively are 'peafowl.' These birds aren't native to New England but are kept as ornamental birds on some properties, and occasionally escape to live wild temporarily.
compareHints: Indian Peafowl are the only members of their genus in New England, but compared to their closest relatives in the pheasant family like Wild Turkeys, they're much more colorful and ornate. While turkeys are brown and focus on camouflage, peafowl males are all about showing off with iridescent blues and greens. Both are large ground birds that can fly, but only peacocks have that incredible fan-tail display.
